article_title: The writing abilities of the elementary and grammar school pupils of a city school system measured by the Ayres scale.
citation: King, I., and Johnson, H. (1914). The Writing Abilities of the Elementary and Grammar School Pupils of a City School System Measured by the Ayres Scale. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072531
title: The Ayres scale as a workable instrument for measuring and comparing handwriting legibility across ages, grades and schools
description: The Ayres scale grades handwriting on eight supposed equal steps designated 20 to 90, with three specimen styles (vertical, medium slant and full slant) under each grade; grade 20 is very poor writing and 90 is excellence "seldom attained in the public schools." The article uses it to grade 966 specimens copied "in their ordinary hand," to compare grade with grade, age with age, and school with school, and to test the scale's practicability. It concludes the scale is workable but that subjective judging cannot be fully eliminated.
requirements: Samples must be judged without reference to the age or grade of the child for fair comparison, as the judge did here
Grading remains a difficult task; the article suggests arranging specimens into eight groups by scale grade and comparing within grades for greater accuracy
constraints: Subjective factors in judging cannot be entirely eliminated, though they may be reduced to a small quantity
A single judge may rank a very good specimen too high if it follows a very poor one
target_learners: elementary and grammar school pupils, grades 1–8, ages 6–17
examples: Applied to all grammar and elementary school children of one small city system, yielding 966 specimens from grades 1 to 8
key_sources: King, I., and Johnson, H. (1914). The Writing Abilities of the Elementary and Grammar School Pupils of a City School System Measured by the Ayres Scale. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072531

article_title: Standardized illustrative sentences for the Springfield Spelling List.
citation: David Spence Hill. (1917). Standardized Illustrative Sentences for the Springfield Spelling List. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org
title: Ayres-Hill standardized illustrative sentence list for the Springfield spelling scale
description: A published instrument pairing words of the Ayres Springfield list with uniform illustrative sentences, printed grade by grade from Grade 3 to Grade 8 (e.g., "Let us fill the pail with sand." for FILL). The author offers it so that "Schoolmen, it is hoped, may find the words and the sentences a convenient instrument for further measurements in spelling," together with the compiled results that afford a basis of tentative standardization.
requirements: Use with the Springfield list administration procedure: word pronounced, sentence spoken, child writes the word only
constraints: The list as printed shows slight variations from the original Springfield List and from the versions used in the Butte, Salt Lake City, and Des Moines studies
target_learning_goals: Measurement of spelling achievement using standardized dictated-word tests
examples: Grade 3 through Grade 8 word-and-sentence pairs are printed in the article, from FILL to DECISION
key_sources: David Spence Hill. (1917). Standardized Illustrative Sentences for the Springfield Spelling List. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org

article_title: The Effect of Enriched Creative Activities Program Supported with Aytürk Technique on Creativity Level in Music Courses
citation: Ayşen Ertürkler and Hakan Bağcı. (2019). The effect of enriched creative activities program supported with Aytürk technique on creativity level in music courses. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2019.3692
title: Aytürk Technique
description: The Aytürk Technique, developed by Ertürkler, is an original classroom technique for music and other disciplines built on "a rhythmic table pattern" and drawing "upon brainstorming, mind mapping, educational games, and gallery walk (board) techniques." Students arrange concepts or rhymes in a 16-cell Rhythmic Table and turn it into rhythmic or melodic structures, producing a musical product at the end of every activity. It aims at a participatory, creative and interactive environment in which students imagine, create and express themselves.
requirements: It requires group work and some creativity from each participating student
It requires the teacher to have class management skills
constraints: It may be useless when not associated with the course
It is difficult to use in crowded classes
It is not effective in solving difficult and complicated subjects
Talented students may monopolize; shy students or those with speech disorders may struggle
examples: In the study, an experimental class of 18 students used the technique in 40-minute sessions for 10 weeks, with body percussion and timbre sources such as pens and erasers; an activity titled The Letter Song came in third in Turkey in a Ministry of National Education activity contest
key_sources: Ayşen Ertürkler and Hakan Bağcı. (2019). The effect of enriched creative activities program supported with Aytürk technique on creativity level in music courses. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2019.3692

article_title: The Effect of Enriched Creative Activities Program Supported with Aytürk Technique on Creativity Level in Music Courses
citation: Ayşen Ertürkler and Hakan Bağcı. (2019). The effect of enriched creative activities program supported with Aytürk technique on creativity level in music courses. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2019.3692
title: Use the Aytürk Technique in preschool and elementary music courses to teach rhythm and reinforce course content
description: Based on the study's positive results, the authors propose that "the original technique can be used to teach rhythm, the basic element of music, in music courses, especially in preschools and elementary schools, and reinforce information on the course in other disciplines." They further propose the program for education programs to enable positive change in students' creative thinking tendencies, and recommend increasing arts activities and courses at schools because development of analytical thinking alone does not develop creativity.
requirements: Teachers trained in creative thinking, since teachers play an important role in developing students' creative thinking skills
constraints: The recommendation rests on a single small experimental study with fewer than 30 individuals per group
examples: The technique was disclosed as part of the E-Twinning project, and 76 schools exemplified for its implementation included the technique in their curriculum as project partners
key_sources: Ayşen Ertürkler and Hakan Bağcı. (2019). The effect of enriched creative activities program supported with Aytürk technique on creativity level in music courses. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2019.3692
